transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-21 15:30 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees Maya, Rahul, Tom / Emma, Liam, Sara, Jordan

Summary (auto): Discussed token burn reduction levers (batching, prefix cache), architecture tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated, and pilot success criteria. Agreed to run a short hosted benchmark and share security artifacts.

00:00:05 Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for making time, uh,, quick roll call?
00:00:12 Emma (Timberline CTO): Emma here, Liam, Sara, Jordan on the line. Good to meet you.
00:00:18 Liam (Platform Eng): morning all.
00:00:22 Maya: great, so our goal for today is to understand your traffic and budget constraints and see where Redwood fits — hosted pilot, dedicated, or private. We'll talk unit economics per token and levers we typically pull.
00:00:38 Rahul (Redwood SE): quick intro from me, I run perf and batching work, i'll try not to get too nerdy but expectation is we look at prompt sizes, percent of chat that's short-turn, kv cache opportunities.
00:00:50 Sara (Head of ML): perfect. To start, our workload is short conversation turns, ~40 tokens avg response, 3-4 turns typical. We have 60k monthly MAUs for the beta and target 5m messages/mo for full rollout but that's 6-9 months out.
00:01:10 Jordan (Security): and from security, Timberline requires SOC2 evidence, KMS integration for keys, and EU residency for customer PII.
00:01:20 Maya: good, that helps. what's your current cost baseline? what are you paying today per inference?
00:01:27 Emma: frank, we're mostly prototype on general cloud GPUs, we haven't instrumented per-token. rough spend is $18k/month for dev infra and we expect prod to be around $60k/mo if we go cloud native. budget cap for initial pilot is $15k for two months.
00:01:50 Rahul: ok noted. with 5m messages a month and 40 tokens avg that's 200M tokens. the unit price matters a lot — hosted per-token plus caching and batching can reduce that.

00:02:10 Liam: can you explain the specific levers? we hear batching, caching, quantization but how do they map to our app?
00:02:18 Rahul: sure — batching groups parallel requests to improve GPU throughput, lowers per-token op cost but may add latency. continuous batching does small windows, that helps short-turn chat. caching — prefix or KV cache: for repeated prompts or similar context you can avoid recomputation of early tokens. that yields big savings if your flows repeat system prompts or templates. quantization reduces model size for lower-cost instance types; we usually benchmark quality tradeoffs.
00:02:50 Sara: do you provide suggestions on config? or we have to tune?
00:02:54 Tom: we provide Redwood Optimize suggestions — i.e., we look at logs, recommend batch sizes, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles. for pilots we do the config and show expected per-token delta.
00:03:08 Emma: what's the rough delta between hosted with caching vs no caching? ballpark helps our planning.
00:03:15 Rahul: very ballpark — for chat with lots of repeated system prefixes, caching alone can cut token compute by 15–40%. batching depends on concurrency shape; if you can accept 50–150ms additional latency, batching can give 10–30% cost reduction on throughput-bound workloads. combined could be 25–55% in best cases.
00:03:38 Jordan: are these savings guaranteed? we need predictable cost for procurement.
00:03:42 Maya: we don't guarantee exact percent but for pilots we run workload-specific benchmarks. we can commit to a measurement plan and SLA for latency tiers on Dedicated. hosted has burst policies and predictable pricing tiers.
00:03:56 Emma: we heard about fallback — if hosted is overloaded, do you route to dedicated or degrade quality?
00:04:03 Tom: policy based routing — you can route by latency SLO, cost profile, or region. fallback could be an identical model hosted on dedicated capacity or a smaller quantized variant. that gives resilience; you define fallback in the rollout.
00:04:18 Liam: what about residency? we need EU-only processing for PII. can hosted satisfy that?
00:04:24 Maya: yes, we have region pinning in hosted and Private (VPC) for stricter needs. for EU residency we can do hosted in eu-west regions or Private deployment in your VPC. KMS integration is supported with HSM-backed keys for Private deployments, and hosted can integrate with customer-managed KMS in some enterprise tiers.
00:04:43 Jordan: customer-managed in hosted? are keys ever exposed?
00:04:47 Tom: hosted with customer KMS uses envelope encryption; Redwood doesn't persist raw keys. for the strictest audits we'd recommend Private deployment.
00:04:58 Emma: okay. one blocker is procurement — they want fixed monthly cost rather than per-token wilds.
00:05:04 Maya: that's why Dedicated exists — reserved capacity with monthly commits. you can mix hosted for burst and Dedicated for steady throughput. we can run a cost model that shows break-even points.
00:05:14 Sara: break-even math: at what monthly token volume does Dedicated beat hosted with caching?
00:05:19 Rahul: depends on batch efficiency and residency. rough rule: for steady high QPS with long sessions, Dedicated often wins above tens of millions of tokens per day. for your forecast 200M tokens/mo we should run the model; could be close.
00:05:34 Emma: let's look at pilot sizing — we only have $15k for two months. what can we get?
00:05:40 Maya: for $15k we can do a hosted pilot with 24/7 throughput test for up to a set token cap, plus configuration assistance. we'll propose a token bucket for the pilot; if you want Dedicated we'd need a commit which is larger.
00:05:53 Liam: the token bucket idea — can you throttle or slice usage to stay within budget?
00:05:57 Rahul: yes, you can set per-route quotas, token caps, rate limits, and have automatic fallback when budget is near. that's common for pilots.

00:06:12 Sara: quality monitoring — we need regression alerts tied to prompt sets. do you have eval tooling?
00:06:17 Tom: Redwood has evaluation hooks — we can run prompt sets, measure quality drift, and send alerts if metrics move beyond thresholds. we can store evals in the console and set automatic rollback to previous model version.
00:06:28 Emma: great, procurement will also ask about audit logs and retention.
00:06:32 Jordan: yep — retention policies, who can see content, RBAC.
00:06:36 Maya: Redwood Console offers token-level traces, per-route dashboards, and audit logs with RBAC. retention windows are configurable on enterprise.

00:06:50 Emma: one technical question from our infra lead — if we use hosted and want to later move to Private, how hard is it to migrate models and configs?
00:06:58 Rahul: migration is straightforward: model versions and rollout policies are abstracted. we provide export of prompt/route configs, and the runtime supports the same model formats. private deployments may require network setup and KMS onboarding, which are the longer lead items.
00:07:12 Liam: about benchmarks — we want a 48-hour hosted run that represents our traffic. what's required from us?
00:07:18 Maya: sample traffic profile, a set of representative prompts, SLO targets, and the token cap for pilot. ideally credentials for a test tenant.
00:07:28 Emma: we'll share that. one more: do you support prefilling context server-side, i.e., token-slicing, or do we always send full context to the model?
00:07:37 Rahul: you can do prefix caching and partial KV reuse — we support streaming and partial cache hits. we have examples in the docs. for many chat apps you can keep system prompts server-side and only send dynamic context tokens.

00:07:50 Sara: what about model variants? if we go hosted, can we use open models or only your curated ones?
00:07:55 Tom: hosted has curated catalog of open models and Redwood-verified variants. we can also bring-your-own model on Dedicated/Private in many cases if licensing permits.

00:08:10 Emma: procurement will also push on SLAs — latency SLOs and credits.
00:08:15 Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers. hosted has best-effort latency but predictable performance profiles. we'll include the SLA language in what we send.

00:08:28 Jordan: do you support SAML/SSO integration and SCIM?
00:08:31 Tom: yes both SAML and SCIM for user provisioning and RBAC. we also have audit trails for admin actions.

00:08:40 Emma: ok, thanks. curious about tooling — how visible will per-token cost be to our product folks?
00:08:46 Maya: in the Console we show token-level cost per request, per-model, and per-route. you can break down by user or team if you send metadata.

00:08:58 Liam: any gotchas on billing alignment? we bill per-token plus any Dedicated commit. for pilots we usually provide a fixed pilot package that includes setup and a token allowance.

00:09:12 Sara: let's go into a quick scenario — 100k messages/day, 40 tokens response avg, 50% repeated templates. can you walk through savings?
00:09:22 Rahul: ok — 100k messages * 40 tokens = 4M tokens/day ~120M tokens/mo. with 50% repeat templates, prefix cache might remove half the prompt tokens for those flows, maybe 15% overall token reduction. batching at moderate concurrency gives another 10–20%. so maybe 25–30% reduction in compute cost vs naively sending all tokens.
00:09:48 Emma: and latency impact? we're budget conscious; we want median p95 sub-500ms ideally.
00:09:55 Tom: with continuous batching and small windows we can keep p50 sub-200ms and p95 often under 600ms depending on model size. if you need strict p95 < 500ms you might need Dedicated or smaller models.

00:10:10 Liam: is there a way to trade quality for cost on the fly? e.g., fallback to cheaper model when budget hits threshold?
00:10:17 Rahul: yes, rollout policies can define tiered fallbacks; at budget threshold you can route to a quantized or smaller model, or a cached response. Application logic can also decide.

00:10:30 Emma: procurement question — if we commit to Dedicated, how long is the contract?
00:10:35 Maya: typical reserved capacity is monthly or annual commits. we can do a 3-month test commit for some customers as a middle ground.

00:10:43 Jordan: do you support VPC peering for Private?
00:10:46 Tom: yes VPC peering and on-prem package for air-gapped requirements. for Private we do full KMS integration and audit support.

00:11:00 Sara: metrics we need from the pilot: per-token cost, latency percentiles, cache hit rates, and quality evals.
00:11:06 Rahul: we'll provide those dashboards and a benchmark sheet; i'll include expected delta columns for batching and caching recommendations.

00:11:18 Emma: sounds good. ok, let's talk specifics about the pilot token cap and configuration.
00:11:23 Maya: if we do $15k for two months, we typically allocate a token bucket and prioritize 24/7 throughput for a subset of routes. we can include a 48-hr stress window.
00:11:34 Liam: what token cap should we set?
00:11:36 Rahul: depends on what you want to validate — for general behavior a 48-72 hour run at representative load with 500k tokens/day should show hit rates and batching behavior. for full cost math we'd need a month of normal traffic.

00:11:50 Emma: procurement may ask for fixed liability if pilot exceeds cap.
00:11:54 Maya: we can set hard caps and alerting; overage can be disabled so you won't be billed beyond pilot allotment.

00:12:03 Sara: one more technical: KV cache evictions — how do you size?
00:12:07 Rahul: we size based on session length and unique keys; we provide suggestions. typical short chat uses small kvs per user and TTLs of minutes to hours depending on reuse.

00:12:18 Emma: can we see a sample benchmark spreadsheet?
00:12:21 Maya: yes i'll attach the pilot pricing and the benchmark template after the call.

00:12:26 [Longer discussion about edge cases and request routing for 10 minutes omitted to save time in this transcript export]

00:22:30 Liam: on model licensing, if we want to bring an internal-finetuned model to Dedicated, is that allowed?
00:22:36 Tom: typically yes, subject to licensing for base models. for private deployments we can host your finetuned artifacts. we also support model version pinning and can host model weights in your KMS-backed storage for Private.

00:23:05 Emma: ok procurement also wants to see SOC2 and an architecture diagram of how data flows for hosted vs private.
00:23:12 Maya: we'll share SOC2 attestation and a compliance pack. also the architecture diagram and KMS integration notes.

00:23:30 Sara: let's capture success criteria: 1) per-token cost below $X (they didn't specify a number here in call) 2) p95 latency < 500ms for priority routes 3) cache hit-rate > 20% 4) SOC2 evidence and EU residency confirmed.
00:23:50 Emma: correct. on cost, internal target is to get per-utterance cost under a threshold that keeps monthly spend under $60k at scale.

00:24:02 Rahul: we'll run the cost model and return a break-even curve and expected pilot outcomes.

00:24:12 Jordan: one more security nit — log redaction options? can you redact PII before storing logs?
00:24:17 Tom: yes we have log redaction, redaction rules, and can configure retention for any logs containing PII.

00:24:25 Maya: ok i'll recap next steps: send pilot pricing, attach benchmark spreadsheet, Rahul to stand up hosted benchmark and run 48-72h window, we will share SOC2 + architecture + KMS notes, schedule follow-up week of Apr 5.
00:24:40 Emma: sounds good. thanks.

00:24:45 [Some cross talk]
00:25:00 Maya: anything else from your side?
00:25:03 Sara: curious about if Redwood has tooling to simulate cost savings from caching without running full pilot?
00:25:10 Rahul: we can do synthetic replay on a reduced sample and model cache hit simulations; won't be exact but directionally useful. we'll include that in the deliverables.

00:25:24 Emma: excellent. procurement wants contract template as well.
00:25:28 Maya: will include.

00:25:35 Liam: question on observability data retention costs — will we pay more to keep a lot of traces?
00:25:41 Tom: observability retention is an add-on for long-term storage. default pilot retention is short; we can propose an add-on price if you need 12 months retention.

00:25:52 Emma: ok thanks everyone.
00:25:55 Maya: quick note — competitor OtherCloudAI often promises lower per-token but less observability and weaker caching; we had customers migrate when they needed predictable ops.
00:26:06 Jordan: good to know.

00:26:10 [Wrap-up and pleasantries]
00:26:30 Maya: we'll send notes and materials by end of day tomorrow. Rahul, you'll own the benchmark?
00:26:36 Rahul: yes i'll own it. i need sample prompts, traffic profile, and a test tenant.
00:26:44 Emma: we'll get that to you.
00:26:47 Maya: terrific. thank you all, talk soon.
